opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest lesson is that scaling laws are less of a crystal ball and more of a measuring stick. When I started, I had this idea that you could run a handful of small experiments, fit a curve, and then just read off how big your network should be and how many games you need for a given compute budget. And to some extent that works. But what it really taught me is that the curve is only as good as the setup you're measuring.

In Go, especially with a self-play, AlphaZero-style loop, you have all these interacting knobs: the size of the network, the number of MCTS simulations per move, how many self-play games you generate, how much you train on each game before the data goes stale. Classic scaling law work in language modeling is comparatively clean. You have a fixed dataset distribution, you trade off parameters against tokens. In self-play, the data distribution is produced by the model itself, so compute spent on inference is also compute spent on making your training data. That coupling makes "compute-optimal" a much slipperier concept.

So the practical way I started using scaling laws was as a debugging tool. If I change something, say the architecture, the value target, or how I sample positions, does the whole curve shift down, or does it just look better at one scale and then flatten out? A lot of tricks that look great at small scale don't change the slope; they just give you a constant offset that disappears as you add compute. And some things that look neutral at small scale actually improve the exponent, and those are the ones worth caring about.

The other thing it taught me is humility about your evaluation metric. If you're fitting curves to training loss, you can fool yourself, because in Go what you ultimately care about is playing strength, Elo against fixed opponents. Those don't always move together. So a lot of the work is just establishing a metric you trust enough that a power-law fit on it means something.

And then, as an individual researcher without a giant cluster, scaling laws are kind of a gift. They let you do meaningful science at small scale and make a reasonable bet about what happens at larger scale, instead of just hoping. You stop asking "is this idea good?" and start asking "does this idea bend the curve?" I think that reframing is the most valuable thing I took away from the whole project.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaling laws as useful for measuring and comparing experiments, but does not state that they are most useful once the underlying method already works.

r002.rationale: It explains that fitting curves from small experiments and observing how changes shift the curve or slope can reveal how the self-play system behaves.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the Go bot project started almost as a side quest. I wanted to understand scaling laws from the inside rather than just reading the Kaplan paper or the Chinchilla paper and nodding along. Go is a really nice sandbox for that because the environment is cheap, the rules are fixed, and you can generate essentially infinite data with self-play. So the question I was asking was: if I have a fixed budget of GPU-hours, how should I split it between a bigger network, more self-play games, and more MCTS rollouts per move? Those are three axes, and nobody had really given me a clean recipe for trading them off.

The first thing it taught me is that scaling laws are a lot less clean than the plots make them look. In language modeling, you get these beautiful straight lines on a log-log plot because the loss is a smooth, dense signal. In Go, your real metric is win rate or Elo, which is a comparison against other agents, and it's noisy and nonstationary. I'd run a sweep and the fit would look great, and then I'd change one hyperparameter like the learning rate schedule and the exponent would move. So a lot of what I learned was about how much of a "law" is actually just a snapshot of your current recipe. The law is conditioned on everything you held fixed, and you usually don't know which of those things matters.

The second thing is that the useful part of scaling laws is not the prediction, it's the discipline. Once you commit to the idea that you're going to spend your compute optimally, you have to actually measure things at small scale and extrapolate, instead of just training the biggest thing you can afford and hoping. That changes your research process. You stop asking "does this trick help?" and start asking "does this trick change the slope?" A lot of tricks give you a constant offset, which is nice but gets eaten when you scale up. The things worth caring about are the ones that bend the curve. Search is interesting in that way, because at small model sizes the MCTS rollouts are doing most of the work, and as the network gets better the marginal value of each rollout drops. So the optimal allocation shifts as you go, and if you fit a law at small scale and extrapolate naively, you'd overspend on search.

The third lesson, and maybe the most humbling one, is that I was a single person with a few GPUs and the whole exercise reminded me that scaling laws are a tool for people who can't afford to be wrong at the frontier. If you're a big lab, you fit the law on small runs so that your one huge run doesn't blow the budget. For an individual, the main value is intuition. I came out of it with a much better gut feel for what a 10x compute increase actually buys you and how fast returns diminish. And honestly, it made me more skeptical of people who wave scaling laws around as a prediction of what a system will do, rather than as a budgeting tool. The law tells you how loss falls. It doesn't tell you what capability emerges, and in Go that gap is really visible, because a bot can be a hundred Elo stronger and still have the same embarrassing blind spots in ladders or life-and-death situations.

So the summary I'd give is: scaling laws are a way to make your compute spend legible to yourself. They're a great forcing function for honest experimentation, they're mediocre at prediction once you change anything, and they're mostly silent about the stuff you actually care about, which is behavior.

astra-6.text:
It taught me that “compute optimal” is a much more specific question than it initially sounds. In Go, you can spend compute training a better policy, or you can spend it searching at inference time. So you’re not just asking how performance scales with model size. You’re asking how to allocate a budget between learning and search—and the answer depends on how many games you expect the bot to play.

The useful thing about scaling laws is that they force you to make those tradeoffs explicit. You can run small experiments and ask, “If I had ten times more compute, where would I put it?” That’s a much sharper research question than “Can I make this agent stronger?”

But the danger is treating a fitted curve as an explanation. Your curve describes a particular algorithm and training setup over the range you measured. Change the search procedure or how you generate training data, and you may change the curve. So I think scaling laws are really useful for allocating resources within a recipe. They’re less reliable as a guide to which new recipe you should invent. You still have to do the research.

r002.rationale: It says a fitted curve describes a particular algorithm and setup, while cautioning that the curve is not an explanation. It does not say data from a working system provides a basis for understanding how that system works.

sol-6.1.text:
The main thing is that a scaling law is conditional on your training setup. It tells you how to allocate compute given a particular algorithm, architecture, and distribution of data. It doesn’t tell you that those choices are good.

With Go, there’s this interesting allocation problem: you can spend more compute training the network, or you can spend more compute searching at inference time. And those interact. A stronger network changes how useful search is, so you can’t necessarily optimize each component independently and expect the whole system to be compute-optimal.

The way I think about scaling laws is as a tool for designing experiments. You do some inexpensive runs, estimate what’s improving and at what rate, and use that to decide which larger experiment is worth doing. But you also want experiments that could invalidate your extrapolation. Otherwise, it’s very easy to spend a lot of compute precisely optimizing within a setup that you should have changed in the first place.
